one_liner: Pure-Zig CPU tensor/autograd runtime and GGUF LLM engine; outruns llama.cpp's CPU backend on most dense Qwen3 prefill shapes.
what_it_does: Fucina is an eager tensor and autograd library in Zig 0.16 with axis names checked at compile time. In-tree applications built on it run GGUF models: Qwen3 dense and MoE, Qwen3.5, Gemma 4, DeepSeek V2/V3/V4 Flash and GLM-4.5, plus speech and vision ports, LoRA and evolution-strategies fine-tuning, and an OpenAI-compatible server (lmserve). You consume it as a Zig package (zig fetch, modules fucina, fucina_models, fucina_serving) or through its zig build CLIs. It reads the same GGUF files as llama.cpp but has no llama.h-style C API.
how_it_is_fast: Hand-written Zig @Vector kernels are specialised at compile time for the host ISA (NEON/sdot on Apple Silicon, AVX2/AVX-VNNI on x86). Quantized weights are repacked into interleaved RHS layouts (for example Q5_Kx8) whose arithmetic is byte-exact with ggml's block formats, f16 GEMMs accumulate in f32, and attention is query-tiled with an online softmax. MoE layers use a 'phased chain' scheduler over routed token-expert pairs (engaged from 64 pairs) with small-m column chunking, and experts are copied into resident packed buffers at load instead of read through mmap. Execution is eager with a reusable buffer pool and no graph or fusion pass. On the M1, part of the prefill margin is llama.cpp's own switch to Accelerate/AMX at batch >= 32, which costs it heavily at pp32-129.
when_to_use: CPU-only Qwen3 dense GGUF inference (0.6B-1.7B measured) on Apple Silicon or AVX2/AVX-VNNI x86, where prompt prefill at 1-256 tokens dominates: dense prefill geomeans 1.18-1.81x on M1 Max and per-format medians 1.32-1.95x on an i9-13950HX
Zig projects that want an in-process tensor, autograd and LLM stack with no C/C++ build system and no Python runtime
CPU training and fine-tuning experiments on the same weights you serve (LoRA on a quantized Qwen3 GGUF at about 932 ms/step for 0.6B on M1 Max, per README)
MoE checkpoints larger than RAM through --moe-stream (README: Qwen3-235B and DeepSeek V4 Flash decode on a 64 GB machine)
Copy-heavy generation (grounded copy, code edits), where its draft-free lossless speculative decoding gave 1.12-2.3x
when_not_to_use: GPU serving: the runtime is eager and offloads to Metal or CUDA only at the GEMM seam, and the README says it will never reach TensorRT-class GPU throughput

MoE decode or Q4_K-expert models: llama.cpp stays ahead on MoE decode (0.87-0.95x on M1, 0.971-0.972x on x86) and on pp256 with Q4_K-transcoded experts (about 15-17% behind); Gemma-4-26B small-batch prefill is 0.85-0.99x on x86, and mid-batch prefill on M1 is listed as an open gap at 0.72-0.91x
Architectures outside its model list; llama.cpp covers far more families and backends
Code that needs a stable API or toolchain: pre-1.0 ('Expect churn') and pinned to Zig 0.16.0 exactly
Memory-tight hosts: experts are copied into resident packed buffers rather than mmap'd, and dense Q5_K weights are held twice (GGUF blocks plus the Q5_Kx8 pack)

integration.dependencies: none required (build.zig.zon has no dependencies); optional BLAS (Accelerate default on macOS; MKL, OpenBLAS or BLIS auto-detected on native Linux), optional Metal or CUDA offload (cuBLAS loaded with dlopen, vendored PTX), optional vendored llguidance (-Dllguidance=true)
integration.min_toolchain: Zig 0.16.0 exactly (minimum_zig_version in build.zig.zon; README: other versions will not build)
integration.platforms: Tuned for aarch64 NEON/dotprod (Apple Silicon) and x86-64 AVX2/AVX-VNNI; a scalar reference backend covers other CPUs; CI runs ubuntu-latest and macos-15; the build targets the host CPU, so cross builds need -Dcpu
integration.thread_safety: Not documented beyond a thread-safe reusable buffer pool (README Design) and a bounded worker team (default 8, build-time ceiling 1-64)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — it reads the same GGUF files and lmserve speaks the OpenAI chat-completions and responses API, but there is no llama.h-compatible C API and only the listed model families load

gotchas: Harness asymmetry on MoE rows: tools/bench_gate.py feeds Fucina a 4-token seed repeated to length N (ids_repeated), while llama-bench feeds uniformly random token IDs (std::rand() % n_vocab in test_prompt). Dense compute does not depend on token content, but MoE routing does. BENCHMARK.md's own profile counters saw only about 52 of 128 Qwen3-30B-A3B experts active per pp256 batch on that prompt, where uniform routing predicts about 124. Fucina therefore streams fewer expert matrices and runs fuller per-expert GEMMs than llama.cpp does on its random prompt, so the MoE prefill ratios (Qwen3-30B-A3B 1.44-2.09x on M1, x86 Q5_K_M pp64-256 1.24-1.30x, Gemma-4-26B) are likely flattered by an unquantified amount; the dense rows are unaffected.

The 'biases every ratio against Fucina' note is overstated. benchOnePass stops the prefill timer before the sampler runs, and the last layer computes only the last query row. llama-bench's generation loop requests logits for every token (batch.add(..., true) in test_gen). The only extra work on Fucina's side is one greedy sample per decode step.

Build defaults matter. -Dmax-threads is a compile-time ceiling defaulting to 8 workers (FUCINA_MAX_THREADS can only lower it), so rebuild for bigger CPUs. Native Linux builds auto-link MKL, OpenBLAS or BLIS when ldconfig lists one, although BENCHMARK.md calls -Dblas=none the default off macOS, so pass -Dblas=none to reproduce the no-BLAS x86 record. Binaries are tuned to the build host, and a bare -Dtarget silently drops the fast kernels.

M1 protocols are mixed. The Gemma-4 and Qwen3.5 rows are Fucina best-of against llama means, and Gemma ran a fresh Fucina process per length against one warm llama process. The Gemma mid-batch scoreboard (1.17-2.15x) comes from a session where llama ran below its own best (pp16 58.4 vs 82.1 tok/s), while the open-gaps list gives 0.72-0.91x.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Fucina over mistral.rs when inference is CPU-only or you want a Zig-native library that also trains: mistral.rs's record is CUDA against llama.cpp's CUDA backend, while Fucina's is ggml's CPU backend. For NVIDIA GPU serving, mistral.rs is the better fit.
verified_claims_summary: Author-run paired comparisons against llama.cpp build 30af6e2 (llama-bench -ngl 0, same GGUF, 8 threads), snapshot 2026-07-04 with 2026-07-10 updates. On an M1 Max (llama.cpp with Accelerate) Fucina led in 221 of 236 prompt-length and decode cells, with dense Qwen3 prefill geomeans of 1.18-1.81x (partly llama's Accelerate switch at batch 32) and dense decode up to +15%. On an i9-13950HX with no BLAS on either side, dense Qwen3-0.6B per-format medians were 1.32-1.95x, while MoE decode, Q4_K-expert pp256 and small-batch Gemma prefill still favour llama.cpp.
